Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the house to-day was moved on the first day of this month by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). It was discussed very ably by hon. members from this side of the house, as well as those from the Progressive, Labour and Independent groups, but Liberal members observed a discreet and possibly ominous silence. None of them has yet indicated his reaction to this resolution. Coming in at this time, when we are in the midst of an unusual depression, at a time when there is considerable u'nrest in the country, the resolution has created a great deal of interest in the house and country. On account of the new political party sponsoring it, and the acclaim the party has received, the resolution has produced the impression in the
1944	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Anderson
minds of some people that it challenges our democratic institutions. It is for that reason only that I venture into the debate.
The first clause deals with the unprecedented unemployment situation obtaining in Canada and in other lands. There is no doubt that everyone regrets the extreme unemployment and the attending distress suffered by many of our citizens. The unemployment situation which we have has been produced by many forces. They are world-wide in their character and have been in operation for some years. I would judge that the great war and the unusual inflation following it, and the unprecedented prosperity from 1921 to 1929, have been largely the causes of our present depression. It commenced in the latter half of 1929 and by the time of the election in 1930 was well under way. It has continued since that time and we are still looking for a solution. This country is not worse off in that regard than other countries, and I compliment the government on the courage and efficiency they have shown in attacking this situation and bringing relief to our unemployed as much as possible.
You may say that the unemployed fall into two classes; the first class, those citizens who never have accepted responsibility for making a living for themselves and providing for their dependents. These people have been on the unemployed list before and probably will be as long as they live. They accept employment by fits and starts but are very much subject to wanting leisure. The second class consists of those citizens who do accept the responsibility of making a living for themselves and providing for their dependents. They are the larger class. The unemployment list to-day includes quite a number who have come on it only this year, because their little savings that they had accumulated in previous years have been spent, and only with great reluctance have they ventured to ask for assistance under the unemployment relief scheme, that is direct relief, that we have this year. This is the class of citizen that deserves sympathy and should get every assistance possible.
Before the present time it has not been looked upon as the duty of the government to provide jobs for the individual. It is the duty of the government to make the laws, to put into effect such machinery as will enforce them, to see to it that the individual's rights and liberty and life are protected, that he is given justice as between man and man. It is the duty of the citizen to obey those laws, to provide for himself as far as possible and to assist in paying the taxes that will keep the country solvent. Many of the people

who are on the unemployed list to-day are not able to pay taxes, but they have paid taxes before and it is not their fault that at present they are not able to do so. It has been said in this house that large numbers of people in this country have been denied the right to work. This is a free country and the right is not denied to any person to work in any vocation he chooses. But circumstances may be such that if they depend for their day's labour on the ingenuity and initiative of some Other individual, under the circumstances we have to-day that other individual may be unable to give them employment. To my mind employment is not going to get much better in the future. We have a condition, brought about by many forces, as I have already indicated, that will render employment in factories and other places not so extensive as in the past.
The unemployment relief system which we have to-day is not satisfactory, it is not a permanent solution for our difficulties. It will be a less satisfactory solution in the future, and I am going to offer a suggestion to the government that I have not heard mentioned before. I do not know of any country that has put anything like it into effect. It is this, that the government should set up some means by which more people will be returned to the land. The government has made some efforts in that direction; I compliment them on it. It is the right direction. They are putting certain people on crown lands in various parts of the country. They are assisting them to make homes and provide for themselves. But I would go further than that. There are large tracts of land going back to a state of nature all over this country. In Ontario -il speak of it particularly-there are large tracts of land unused at the present time farms practically deserted. You see them in all sections, with only a fence around the hundred acres, no fences within, going back to grass and weeds. I would suggest that the money that is now spent on unemployment relief might be better used in acquiring some of that land by the government, parcelling it out into small lots, five or ten acres, or even twenty-five acres, and taking the unemployed from our cities, towns and villages and putting them on that land; assist them by giving them expert direction, and help to build their own homes. Show them how to produce agricultural products by what might be called a forced system. If numbers of these people were given the opportunity to go on the land -and I know lots of them would be willing- they could produce on a five acre lot all the fruit and vegetables they require. They could also produce eggs and poultry, milk and butter,

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Anderson
sufficient fodder for the cow and grain for their fowl. Then they would have a stake in the country, would be more contented, and better citizens. It would provide a solution in a certain measure of the unemployed situation to-day.
I would also suggest that some of the large industrial plants move from the cities to country districts where they might be surrounded by land which could be parcelled out amongst the employees in a similar manner. The day is coming when fewer men will be employed in those industrial plants, the shorter working day and week are coming, so they are going to have more leisure time. It would be a good plan to give them a stake in the country, where they could use their leisure in doing something for themselves, improving their homes. It would keep them from burning up gas on the highways and getting into traffic jams, and I am quite satisfied that they would be happier, and better citizens, and would be less troublesome in times of distress. I simply offer this to the government as a suggestion in the hope that it may be looked into and if possible put into operation to a certain extent.
In the second or main section of the resolution is embodied the policy of the new political party. I will read it:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately take measures looking to the setting up of a cooperative commonwealth in which all natural resources and the socially necessary machinery of production will be used in the interests of the people and not for the benefit of the few.
That, of course, is plainly a socialistic program. This new party, as stated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his speech on February 1, has attracted to itself certain other groups and political parties in this country. Those affiliated are the United Farmers of the three prairie provinces and of the province of Ontario, but I note that the United Farmers joined with a reservation. They got into bed with the new party, but indicated that should the sleeping conditions prove not congenial they would leave at any time. They intimated that in affiliating with the new party they still maintained the right to follow their own policies as United Farmers. Speaking of the United Farmers of Ontario more particularly, I may say that they are a hardheaded business class and very shrewd politicians. They are not going into anything very definitely and securely until they know how it is going to turn out, and just so soon as they find out what this commonwealth actually means a great number of them will secede from it.
Not only that, but even at the present time the leaders who have affiliated with the new party will not be able to carry with them anything like the body of United Farmers of Ontario. It is also stated that the labour unions from the Pacific coast to the border of Quebec have affiliated with this new organization. Well, the labour unions may have affiliated but there is a large class of labour in the dominion that does not belong to the union. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made the statement, that they had affiliated.

I think the hon.
gentleman is in error; I said nothing about the labour unions.

If the hon.
gentleman says they have not, I will accept his word. But I find at page I6S8 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
Further than that, the political labour bodies in the provinces from British Columbia to Montreal have also voted to affiliate.
That gave me the impression that he meant the labour union, but apparently he meant something else. He also said that there were a large number of people in this country who had indicated their intention of uniting with the party, people from one end of the country to the other, and I have noticed in the newspapers that many people have so intimated. There was also another party, it appears, that endorsed the policy of the new party and which neither the hon. gentleman nor any member of his party mentioned, and that was a section of the United Church of Canada. The United Church in Toronto on December 7, 1932, in their report presented to the Presbytery of that city, moved this resolution which was passed:
In view of the fact that our political leaders have not evolved any adequate system so far as the masses are concerned, but have _ directed their efforts toward protecting vested interests, rather than the common welfare, be it resolved that we adopt some such program as that of the C.C.F.
Hear, hear.
Hon. gentlemen say " hear, hear," but large numbers of the United Church of Canada do not say " hear, hear."
Hear, hear.

And the
United Church itself does not say "hear, hear." Now, the acceptance of this policy as presented by hon. members across the aisle will simply mean that we shall need to get a new constitution for the dominion.

Hear, hear.

I am glad
they say " hear, hear " to-day, but the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not say "hear, hear" when that was said on the first of this month by the Prime Minister. He did not believe then that it would be necessary to change the constitution of the country if the policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation was to go into effect. The policy as enunciated is communist, pure and simple. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the party behind him are sincere in what they say. They are in favour of socialism or communism, and the difference between these two systems was defined in the house by the hon. gentleman: communism is brought in by force and the other by constitutional means. I agree with the hon. gentleman in that statement; so far as I can make out from a study of the two systems, that is the difference. But can anyone supporting an effort towards socialism say that force will not eventuate? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not say that force could be prevented. At page 1689 of Hansard, in answer to a question that was asked at the time, as to whether force might be used, he said:
It may very well be that force may prove inevitable, yes, if the attitude of certain gentlemen is persisted in and the people of this country are denied the right that they have to self-expression and to the enjoyment of a decent livelihood.
That is the statement of the hon. gentleman, that force will be used if it becomes inevitable. Now, that is a warning and also a threat.

Did he say who was
going to use force?

No, but who else except the socialist party? Does the hon. gentleman think that the rest of Canada will use force? The hon. member made this statement that I have quoted. This means that if the people of the dominion are docile enough to accept this policy meekly, if they do not resist, then we shall have socialism; but if the rest of us do resist, if the people object to it, we shall have force, because in any event this party intends to put its policy into effect and create a socialistic or communistic state in this country.
The hon. gentleman is misstating entirely the position I took the other day.
It is a fair deduction.

I am basing my proposition upon the statement made by the hon. gentleman himself. That is the way it appeared to me and I am satisfied that is the way it will appear to many other people in Canada. If the hon. gentleman did not mean that, I am sorry that I misconstrued his remarks as I have no desire to do him wrong. It is the intention of this new party which had its birth in the closing months of 1932, to appeal to the electorate upon this policy. That is their whole policy because it has been stated in this house and it has not been enlarged upon. It is a policy fashioned after the Russian system, it is nothing less than that.
The hon. gentleman gravely asks this parliament to endorse this policy and put it into effect immediately. That is a most extraordinary proposition to make to any house. Such a proposition makes it impossible for any hon. member, no matter how favourable he may be towards that policy, to vote to put it into effect immediately. That would not be democratic. It is socialistic to ask that we go ahead without the endorsation and consent of the people of Canada. Such a course of action would wreck our constitution and destroy confederation.
The hon. gentlemen who are advocating this policy state that it is meant to displace capitalism. It might displace capitalism but it would destroy democracy. What is eapital-sm? It is simply a system by which we produce wealth for the production of further w'ealth. Capitalism as we know it to-day came into being during the last half of the nineteenth century, less than one hundred years ago. Since that time the world has made more progress than it had in the previous five thousand years. The success of capitalism has been phenomenal; the world jumped ahead immediately it came into effect and the progress of the world has been continuous ever since. As the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) said, when this system was founded the world was suffering from a scarcity of everything except poverty, but in less than a century we had an overproduction and over-abundance of everything. In spite of this, capitalism is denounced as a failure. Before capitalism terrible famines took place all over the world. I can remember when the people of Ireland faced starvation because of the failure of the potato crop and I can remember when the people of India and China were starving by the millions because of the failure of their crops. What has been

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Anderson
the result of capitalism? Famine has been eliminated, so much so that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin says that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation offers economic independence to everybody.

My statement was that
economic security was offered to everyone.

The hon.
member is reported on page 1743 of Hansard of February 2, as saying;
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation guarantees to every Canadian economic independence.
If there has been a mistake made in Hansard the hon. gentleman should have had it corrected. He said also that there was in this country sufficient plant and equipment to guarantee at least an abundance of the necessaries to every Canadian. That would mean that the Canadian people would have economic independence and an abundance of necessaries free of cost. It is the intention of hon. gentlemen to destroy the price system and to destroy capitalism, consequently the necessaries of life, which include shelter, clothing, food and heat and light, will be given free to everybody. Was there ever a greater slogan for an election? Was there ever a greater attempt at wholesale bribery of the people? Such promises are over and above any ever made by the Liberal or Conservative parties, yet hon. gentlemen complain about the promises made by the political parties during election campaigns.
In the last twenty-five years-I make this statement subject to correction if any hon. member cares to correct me-the world made more advancement under capitalism than it had made in the previous two thousand years. Does any hon. member want to deny that statement? Since the war everything has been stimulated by capital. Laboratories were set up wherein scientists could work unhampered by the necessity of producing a living. Nature has been made to yield up her secrets and those secrets have been applied to such an extent that our civilization has been transformed. Yet, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, capitalism is a huge failure.
Capitalism brought in the machine age in which we are now. By means of the capital expended in the laboratories, in our industries and in all lines of personal endeavour, the machine has been developed to such an extent as to eliminate thousands of men from gainful labour. Far more men have been eliminated than is required to build the machine. This has all been brought about by 53719-1231
capital. We are entering the electrical age, our machines are going to be run by electricity and more men will be eliminated from gainful occupations. These things are just signs of the times, they are progress and it is futile for anyone to think that he can stop the progress of the world. It will go ahead in spite of what any human being may do.
What is happening to those men who have been eliminated?

I am just
going to take up that point. The hon. gentleman gave his own solution for this. I am not saying that there is nothing in socialism,
I am simply saying that we are on the verge or are well advanced into a new era. The sun of that new era is well above the horizon and the signs of the time are everywhere for any man to read. We are not going back to the old system but also we do not need to go to socialism. We can carry on with the system we have, that is capitalism. The only thing that is wrong now is that capitalists did not realize that the advances have been so great that it is out of step with our social order. Capitalism got ahead of the social order which we have in the world to-day and we must bring the social order up in step with capitalism.
The machine age is only beginning. As I have said, we shall see further advances and progress in machinery until possibly some day every man will be able to have a servant of an electrical character. That is one of the possibilities of the future and we must prepare for it. But only a fanatic would attempt to disrupt the present order by trying to bring in a new order all at once. If there is to be a new order, it must come gradually and imperceptibly, a merging of the old into the new, so that when the old order passes out, the new order will be ready to take charge of the situation and carry on. I am not altogether advocating capitalism. I say that it has been a splendid thing for the world, but it has defects. It has had defects which have been remedied; the defects which it now has can be remedied, and by remedying those defects and carrying on with our present progress we shall eventually bring about a system under which the people of this world will be able to have a living without very much work. We shall be able to have abundance to eat and all the luxuries of life without having any socialistic state. Socialism was in existence long before capitalism. Socialism has been in existence pretty nearly as long as the world has. It is a failure in

*Russia to-day, and it is a peculiar situation for some hon. members to be advocating socialism and communism when socialism and communism are at this very time failures in Russia. Russia started out without a price system. They were going to run a socialistic state there by making everybody engage in labour and by parcelling out to them what they needed in the way of food, clothing, shelter and so forth. But what is happening now? At the end of five yearn they are trying to bolster up their plan by bringing in capital. They are beginning to arrange for a capitalistic system in that country to bolster up a system of communism. They are asking the loan of capital from outside countries, even from Canada. Socialism has not been a success; it has been a failure, and all I have to say is that we should stay with the capitalistic system that we have, improve and perfect it, and it will bring us out of the depression in which we find ourselves just at present.

attribute to the hon. gentleman anything that he has not at least implied. He asks how this thing can be brought about. What thing? He answers his own question by saying that it has been brought about in Russia. Well, will he undertake to say that there is not a dictatorship in Russia, the most ruthless, the most cruel dictatorship that has ever been known in history? And he says himself that this thing, which he had been talking about for two hours to the people of Port Arthur, has been brought about in Russia; true, by the slaughter of millions of people and with intense suffering. And he frankly tells the people of Canada, on the floor of the House of Commons, that force will be used by this dictatorship to bring about the same situation.

Mr. Speaker, the
hon. member is misquoting me; I never said such a thing. I ask that the statement be withdrawn.

It is not a point of
order for one hon. member to contradict another. If the hon. member wishes to deny a statement made by someone else in debate, or to point out wherein he has been misquoted, he can do so when he comes to reply.

I have been
charged with having made certain statements in the House of Commons, which statements I did not make.

That is not a point of
order.

I insist that it is
a point of order. A statement has been made which is not true and I ask that it be withdrawn.

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Nicholson

There is no point of
order in that.

I ask that the
statement be withdrawn, because it is not true.
It is certainly not what we have to-day.

Stable currency is a currency which is accepted at par in any country in the world, but you are not going to get it by any effort on the part of ten millions of people in the face of the whole world, simply by starting to issue fiat money or an inflated currency.

You certainly have not got stable money now.

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Nicholson

Sir Basil Blackett goes on to say:
If I put stable money in the forefront of what is needed for successful national reconstruction, it is because national planning ahead is so difficult as to be almost impossible without reasonable stability of prices.
Price stability is really stable money.

Price stability will be arrived at when we get stable money throughout the world-then and then only. Hon. gentlemen opposite to my right are always asking for stable money. Sir Basil Blackett says:
With stable money, industry can concentrate anew on bringing down the costs of production.
Sir William Beveridge says:
The third point is that this crisis is a world crisis, a common disaster of all the world. As such, it is a disaster that is only going to be made worse if each nation thinks purely nationally, thinks or acts in a narrow, selfish spirit.
We have heard a great deal about what happened when England went off the gold standard, and England's currency became inflated, as people say. As a matter of fact, England did not go off the gold standard in the sense of voluntarily leaving it. She went off the gold standard simply because she was forced off it.
Mr. VALLAN'CE: In just the same position as Canada, only Canada won't go off it.
No, she won't as long as we can carry on our business, and as long as we remain sane.
Your dollar is fictitious now.

Again, Sir William
Beveridge says:
Some people have hailed our going off the gold -standard as a means by which we can damage the trade of other people and benefit our own. *Going off the gold standard has helped us in certain ways, but it has thrown the trade of the world still more into confusion.
Every step that is taken in that direction to unstabilize currency and world trade makes it just that much more difficult for the nations of the world, Canada included, to get back into the position they were in before. As Sir William Beveridge says:
The small, immediate gain to us on one side has been offset on the other side by loss to the world and to us as in the world.
The trouble is that some hon. gentlemen who in and out of season have demanded that we should broaden our outlook and trade
with the world have now come forward with the proposal that we should draw ourselves into our shell and establish a credit and currency system that will be effective and useful in Canada, but of no use whatsoever beyond our shores.
One more word from Sir William Beveridge, and then I shall have finished with quotations from this book:
So I, for my part, come back to seeking a way out of the world's crisis within the frame work of the capitalistic system, by suppressing, through international cooperation, the anarchy of purchasing power-by suppressing the anarchy of purchasing power and keeping and increasing the liberty of production and exchange. That is the way of escape.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) referred to a statement concerning capitalism made in the House of Lords by Lord Marlev. In that same speech Lord Marley made statements similar to the one made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at Port Arthur, that "there ia no unemployment in Russia." Another gentleman spoke in the House of Lords-I refer to Lord Snowden, parts of whose speech were quoted this afternoon. In a newspaper article before me he is quoted, in part, as follows:
At such times there have always been those who are proclaiming the collapse of the capitalist system.
Well, the system is not going to end just yet. Some of my socialist friends have never realized the tremendous recuperative power of capitalism.
Some hon. members in this house have never realized the tremendous recuperative power of the individual Canadian who, in his own way, is determined to work out his own destiny and not be subjected to the dictatorship of hon. members opposite. The article continues:
And we shall see ourselves through this crisis, although, mark you, I am not in the least ignoring the importance of changes in-to use the phrase of noble Lords opposite-our plan of national organization and national reconstruction. But I certainly cannot follow the noble Lord, Lord Marley, in going to Russia for an example. The noble Lord said that there are no unemployed in Russia. I do not think lie would find many unemployed in Dartmoor jail.
This is the statement of Lord Snowden, the man who has been hailed as the greatest socialist in England. The article continues:
Russia is under a system of industrial conscription. Russia has confiscated all the capital, repudiated all public debts, and yet, starting without any capital liability at all, Russia has ever since been coming to the capitalist countries of the world cap in hand, begging them for export trade and loans.

1078	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Mitchell
We have had a recent example of that in Canada, if we can be guided by statements from Serkau and his friends, who have come to us and asked us to buy goods, and pay cash for them.
Time is up.
I should like to speak a moment more.

The hon. member has
spoken for forty minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member who preceded me that probably the fewer the quotations, the product of other peoples' brains, made by hon. members, the better will be the discussion. This House ol Commons is a fairly accurate cross section of the men and women who comprise the population of this broad dominion. It must reflect the moods and desires of those men and women. I believe that individuality may be better shown by accepting responsibility for our own statements than by reading from books the statements of others.
During the course of this debate we have heard the statements of hon. members both to the right and the left of Mr. Speaker who are suffering from the Russian jag. We have to take a realistic viewpoint of what is going on in that country, the forces that brought about the revolution, and the reasons for it, with which the Russian people and no others were thoroughly familiar. That country will work out its own destiny in its own way. May I observe that while in Russia there is poverty amidst scarcity, in this broad dominion there is poverty amidst plenty.
Which is better?
Some one has asked which is better. I reply that poverty amidst plenty is at least a challenge to our good sense and our leadership.
Is it?

I believe it was the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) who made the observation a few evenings ago that this resolution was a challenge to democracy. I believe the challenge to democracy comes from the other side of the house. Certainly democracy would be challenged if the attitude of the men and women in constituencies such as West York were truly reflected by the statements made by their representatives in the House of

Commons. Members of the house have been forbidden to speak in the city of Toronto. Then they say that this resolution is a challenge to democracy. We have heard a great deal about freedom of speech. I have fixed opinions along that line; if I had my way there would be a forum in every town and hamlet of Canada in which men and women could express their opinions unfettered by those who disagreed with them. That is a good old British custom. I have before me a clipping which gives an account of a parade of 100,000 people which only a few days ago passed through the city of London and held a meeting concerning unemployment. If they can do that in Great Britain, it is only reasonable that we should be allowed to do it here. I want to say, however, that freedom of speech carries with it responsibilities. I do not believe any individual or group of individuals who preach the overthrow of democractic institutions, as we know them have a right to that freedom of speech. In my judgment it is only logical the democratic institutions should protect themselves from forcible overthrow. There is in my opinion a licence for freedom of speech. I make that observation because the statement is made that labour members are to some extent connected with the Third Internationale. I want to make this perfectly clear, that there is as much difference between the labour movement of this country and the tactics of the Third Internationale as there is between atheism and Christianity.
What is the difference?

I think we will all
agree that very few know what the future holds for this country, or any other country for that matter. Fundamental changes have to be made to meet the problems that confront us. Within the precincts of this house a man that the Prime Minister of this country admitted was one of the brightest financial minds in the world to-day, Sir Josiah Stamp, made the observation, and members of this house applauded it, that he felt that we shall reach a stage halfway between our system and the Russian system. That is the opinion of a responsible man of the world who at least knows the way he is going.
Some have spoken of confiscation. Good heavens, why talk about confiscation? It is going on all around us. Among the people I pass my life with, their houses and everything they possess is being confiscated at this very moment, through circumstances over which they have absolutely no control. Yet hon. members talk about confiscation. I want.

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Mitchell
to say this, speaking for myself as an individual and without undertaking to represent the viewpoint of the labour movement of this country, that I am absolutely opposed to confiscation by the state. Any man who would suggest such a thing is not in his right senses, in my judgment.
Oh, oh.

I am looking at you.
I believe the changes contemplated by this resolution should be made gradually and through the recognized constitutional channels. I believe they must be founded on conviction and on enlightened public opinion. I would remind you that cooperation or collective effort brought us through the greatest conflict in history, enabled the countries of the commonwealth to emerge successfully from the most destructive war that we know of. That is why I believe that the resolution is not so destructive as implied by some hon. members who have taken part in this debate. The hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) who spoke the other evening and said so much about the rights of the individual, I understand is a lawyer by profession-
That is no crime.

Someone says it is no
crime. But I want to say this, that the legal profession has developed out of the control of the individual by the state, in the progress of mankind from his lowliest stage up to the present. It deals with the law which controls the individual, defends him, prosecutes him, within the framework of the state. I sincerely believe that social control has made a greater contribution to the life of the people of this and all civilized countries than did the rank individualism that some people would have us drift back to.
I believe .this depression has reached the stage at which plain language should be used. I believe that one can love his country and yet use plain language and face facts. Some people think that a kind Providence is going to stick his hands through the clouds and pull the chestnuts out of the fire for us. Gentlemen, it is not done that way. We got ourselves into this difficulty and we have got to think ourselves out of it.

What are you going to do
about it?

I will -come to that in a minute. I am not unmindful of the difficulties that stand in the way of the ultimate realization of the principles enunciated in this resolu-53719-125i
tion. I believe they will have to be met, as other problems in life, by trial and error. I believe that the social and economic forces of this -country are subject to -change, the same as any biological organism. We have had change sin-ce the dawn of history, improvement in social conditions, cultural conditions. More ample educational facilities have been provided. Surely few among those who strenuously opposed this resolution appreciate how far we have progressed from nineteenth -century individualism towards the ultimate adoption of the principles enunciated in this resolution. In my judgment .public control and regulation as they -have developed are all to the good of the body politic. In the province I come from we have the hydro-electric system, one of the greatest examples of practical cooperation on-e could wish to see, though I may say that it -may be wrecked by the private ownership mentality that we have seen displayed recently in the absorption of the assets o:f the Dominion Power an-d Transmission Company and the Abiti-bi Power and Paper Company. Such incidents have the power to destroy the influence of that wonderful undertaking. Then we have the Canadian National Railways, often criticized by hon. members here, but I think you will agree with -me that it was taken over by this -country because private enterprise completely fell -down. We had reached the stage where no money could be made out of it and the child was left on the doorstep of the Canadia-n people. Personally I still believe that the Canadian National Railways will reflect credit on this country when we return to more normal times.
Then there -is the radio, as mentioned by my colleague, the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. He-a-ps). In medicine again we have a good example of the desire of the individual to make some contribution to the wellbeing of his time, where the incentive- is not profit. Think of such men as Mackenzie, Osier, Pasteur, Harvey and Lister: thse men made great contributions to the science in which they were engaged-, and they did so without any hope of enormous rewards. I have often thought that if the problems -that affect us economically and socially were attacked with the- same vigour and with the same high ideals in view, for the uplift of men- and women in this dominion, we should soon be out of the trouble in which we find ourselves at the present time. Medicine knows no country; in fact, the profession lays down the principle that any discovery made by one of its members must be passed on for the good of all mankind.
Take the question of public health. Here great strides have been made. Lives have
1980	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Mitchell
been, saved through the insistence of the state that the scourges that afflict mankind shall be eliminated. There are one or two figures which I would give with regard to my own city, to show the effect of medicine on public health as expressed in a cooperative way in that community. In 1905 the annual death rate was 14-4 per thousand, and in 1932, 9-4; the infant death rate in 1905 was 158-5 per thousand children born alive, and in 1932, 56-7 phr thousand. In connection with tuberculosis the death rate in 1905 was 120-9 and in 1932, 43-2, and in 1905 there were 20 deaths from typhoid fever whereas in 1932 there was but one death, and this person was infected while out of the city. Diphtheria has been practically eliminated.
A question has been raised with respect to the constitutional difficulties that confront the country in meeting the problems that have arisen from the depression. I am not unmindful of this but I would point out that it is constitutional difficulties that sometimes kill the individual. I believe that the constitution of this country as embodied in the British North America Act is just as amenable to change as anything else. The fathers of confederation, living as they did in a world where transportation and communication were so much slower than they are to-day, did a remarkably fine job; but if the problems arising in our industrial and agricultural structure in the year 1933 are to be met, I think it is absolutely necesary that the act be amended to cope with many of these problems on a national rather than a provincial basis.
History has taught us that it is best to build on experience and tradition rather than to trust entirely to abstract principles. It is seldom possible to predict what will happen under new conditions. Taking a broad point of view of the difficulties that face us to-day, I am of the opinion that there are two avenues of approach to our problem. We have either to scrap the present industrial system and go back to industry on a smaller scale and more individualism, through pure economics of laissez faire, or we have to plan and utilize our potentialities for the maintenance of the present productivity of the country. In this connection I would quote a passage from the report of the committee which was appointed by President Hoover to deal with social trends. The report states:
The committee suggests that there might in time emerge a national advisory council, including scientific, educational, governmental, economic (industrial, agricultural, and labour) points of contact, or other appropriate elements, able to contribute to the consideration of the basic social problems of the nation. Such an agency might consider some fundamental questions of the social order, eoonomic,

governmental, educational, technical, cultural, always in their interrelation, and in the light of the trends and possibilities of modern science.
It is clear that the type of planning now most urgently required is neither economic planning alone, nor governmental planning alone. The new synthesis must include the scientific, the educational, as well as the economic (including here the industrial and the agricultural) and also the governmental. All these factors are inextricably intertwined in modern life, and it is impossible to make rapid progress under present conditions without drawing them all together. . . . Fully realizing its mission, the committee does not wish to assume an attitude of alarmist irresponsibility, but on the other hand it would be highly negligent to gloss over the stark and bitter realities of the social situation, and to ignore the imminent perils in further advance of our heavy technical machinery over crumbling roads and shaking bridges. There are times when silence is not neutrality, but assent.
The foregoing is from Review of Reviews and World's Work, arising out of the report of the committee appointed by President Hoover, and this is the comment of the reviewer:
To all those who contributed to the success of the committee's work, and to the committee itself, the volumes will be a lasting credit. Americans may some day have occasion to feel that President Hoover's conception and inauguration of the work marked one of the high-points in his presidential career.
In my judgment, the state must take the lead. We find today that the leaders in finance and industry have fallen down. They are busy handing out advice and at the same time putting on the brakes on any governmental action. I am firmly convinced that so great is the drive of circumstances and events that the impetus to * collectivism cannot be checked. Men and women of all schools of thought see the inevitable logic in this; they realize that this must happen if civilization is to be saved. In my opinion the state is the only Stable thing left, it must be said in fairness that the state is one of the few institutions which has not gypped the investor. If I may visualize the drift of events, I see the establishment as part of our national life of agencies to direct and plan industrial stabilization, to establish minimum prices, to set up standards of quality, to reform the monetary system and to subordinate credit to industrial needs.
Much was said to-day by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) and the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) in connection with Philip Snowden, now Lord Snowden. He received some measure of praise from both speakers. Looking over my files to-day I came across a copy of the debates in the British House of Commons covering a

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Bury
discussion almost identical with that now being held in this house. Apparently we are just ten years behind the times, because this debate was held on March 20, 1923. Mr. Snowden moved the following resolution:
That, in view of the failure of the capitalist system to adequately utilize and organize natural resources and productive power, or provide the necessary standard of life for vast numbers of the population, and believing that the cause of this failure lies in the private ownership and control of the means of production and distribution, this house declares that legislative effort should be directed to the gradual suppression of the capitalist system by an industrial and social order based on the public ownership and democratic control of the instruments of production and distribution.
That government was in power for years after that and Philip Snowden could have put that resolution into effect.
The Liberals had a platform, and so had the Conservatives.

That government could have put that into effect.
Mr. MITCH ELI,: I just make that observation in passing. Those who took part in that debate are well known to hon. members of this house. The participants were Sir Alfred Mond, Mr. E. C. Grenfell, Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Briggs, Mr. Arthur Henderson, and Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, who closed the debate.
A question such as this should be discussed without rancor. I say that because I believe that within the next five years the drift of legislative effort and the functions of parliament will be in the direction of the purport of this resolution. We cannot go back, the niraeteeth century has passed with all its practices. This House of Commons, not necessarily this government, in meeting the problems arising out of mass production and agriculture and industry, will move in the direction of the purport of this resolution. I am not one of those who says that this can be done in a day; I am not one of those who go out and kid the people that that can happen. In 1930 we saw the spectacle of what happened when claims were made that certain things would happen if a certain government was returned to power. I believe we must take an evolutionary course. There are those who say that this civilization will crumble around us, but I want to make this observation:	We
differ fundamentally from such earlier civilizations as those of Greece, Rome and Carthage, which were built upon the sufferings of the great proportion of the population of those days. We have built up a magnificent educational system and that I believe will be the
driving force which will insist that the legislators of this country meet the problem of today, that the machine be controlled instead of permitting the machine to control us. It is even within the realm of possibility that the present government will take some steps in the direction we suggest before it again goes to the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will have observed with a great deal of pleasure that the hon. member who last spoke, the member for East Hamilton. (Mr. Mitchell) is not proposing to support this resolution. As the bon. member for East Algorma (Mr. Nicholson) pointed out. the resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately take measures looking to the setting up of a cooperative commonwealth-
The hon. member who has just spoken evidently is not prepared to endorse the resolution to this extent; the greatest length to which he is prepared to go is to move gradually in that ultimate direction. The house-no doubt also noticed that the hon. member, commencing his remarks by criticizing the hon. member for East Algoma for reading the opinions of eminent economists, ended them by himself reading a long screed from the Review of Reviews.
As a preface to what I wish to say upon the motion, may I assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who is responsible for the motion, that if I refer to his organization by its initials, C. C. F., rather than by its full and formal name of Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, it is not because I wish to disparage in any way the organization, its founder or its supporters, but, because the name is so fearfully and wonderfully made that I distrust my memory. I am rather reminded of the child who was christened by its proud and fond parents, under the impression of a tremendous destiny lying in front of it, with the name Sampson Agonistes Smith. No child could possibly survive that name, especially if, as afterwards happened, a bad attack of rickets left him in the position where 'the mode of his progress was that the right leg had to say to the left, "You let me go by this time and I will let you get by next." Of such an infant the only anticipations any of us could possibly form would be gloomy forebodings of his early demise.
The resolution which the hon. member and his supporters are urging the house and the country to endorse, appears to me to be in essence a conclusion that must depend for
1382	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Bury
its validity upon two premises. The first is that our present social structure and economic and financial system have so completely collapsed thait even if we could restore them, we should not attempt to do so. The second premise is that the new organization, the C. C. F., is capable of doing what the old system failed to do, extracting us from our present situation and insuring us against its recurrence at any future time.
These are two rather extravagant statements to make; but they are the two premisses that are essential to the conclusion of the resolution and both of them must be proved. If the present system has not broken down, then there is no need for us to look for a substitute. If, on the other hand, it has broken down, but the proposed substitute is not able to do any better, then wherever else we may look for a substitute, it will not be in the southeast corner of this chamber. Therefore I disagree with my hon. friend, the member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), eloquent and plausible as he is, in his assertion that it was the present system and not the CiC.F. that was on trial. He kept reiterating that statement so often, that the only impression he left upon me was that he was trying to convince himself of its truth. "We are not on trial," he said, "it is the present system which is on trial." That might be true if the sole aim of those who are urging this resolution on the house were to displace the existing system. But they know they cannot stop there; they cannot leave us with a vacuum. We have not yet arrived- at the splendid isolation of the position of that mythical Ford car which was able after dropping its engine on the road still to keep running on its reputation. We have apparently, according to hon. gentlemen in the southeast comer, no reputation to run on. They are not merely attempting to displace the present system. What they are really attempting to do is to substitute their system for the present one. Under those circumstances, surely the onus rests upon them of proving the validity, w'orth and efficacy of the system which they wish us to adopt.
They are not merely dethroning Charles I and then executing him to prevent the possibility of a monarchical reaction placing him back again on his empty throne, but putting a commonwealth in his place. I may remind my hon. friends that the commonwealth which followed Charles I did not last very long. It lasted practically just the length of the lifetime of one man; and it lasted that long only because he, the man who founded, headed and governed it, was one of the greatest men of his day in England and raised the prestige, name and power of England among the na-

tions of the earth, and yet a man of such broad vision that, despite his theological views, he was able, without any idea of irreverence, to write to the Assembly of the Scottish Presbyterian Church: "I beseech you in the bowels of Christ to think it possible you may be mistaken." The hon. gentlemen come to us really with the suggestion that we should throw out the water we now have because it is dirty and inadequate, and they resent our saying to them: Before we do that, will you please prove to us that the water you wish us to take in its stead is any cleaner or more adequate. We certainly refuse to throw out the water we have, even though it be dirty and inadequate, until we know' we are going -to get in its place something better.
I have listened to some of the speeches that have been made in support of this resolution and have read others of them, and I have yet failed to hear or to read from statements made either inside or outside the house, any real evidence of the truth of either of those two premisses. I invite the house to consider them for a few minutes. Previous speakers and others who will follow me will deal with other aspects of the question, will examine the structure and the principles of the proposed commonwealth with a view to criticizing them and showing their inadequacy, or will deal with other aspects of the subject. I do not propose to take that course; I propose to follow one specific line of thought and to confine myself to it, that namely, suggested by what I have said, that before this house should be persuaded to make any change in the way of the suggested substitution, it should have proved to itself beyond any reasonable doubt the two premises which I have mentioned.
Let us take the first of them: that the present system has so collapsed that it is incapable of functioning, and that even if we could restore it, we should not do so. Is that true? Well, it is certainly true relatively.
I am not going to deny that. Indeed, none of us would deny it. Not that we are opposed to admitting what we know to be true, but we regret that it is true. I have been rather wearied in listening to some of the speeches that have come from the southeast corner of the house, and particularly to the reiterated suggestion of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) and her perpetual question: "I wonder, do hon. gentlemen opposite realize?" Well, we do realize.
I can assure my hon. friends and the lady member for Southeast Grey that neither has she nor have they a corner on the powers of observation or of intellect or of the faculty of sympathy. We both observe and under-

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Bury
stand, appreciate and sympathize with those who are suffering in the present situation. Indeed, some of us think we understand a good deal more about it than do some hon. members who are so careful and anxious that we should properly appreciate the situation. We have seen the suffering which it has induced and continued, not in rural districts where that suffering is least, but where it is worst, in the hearts of some of our cities. We know all that the farming community of this country is suffering; we do not deny they are suffering and we do not deny them sympathy in their suffering and the expression of a determination to do whatever lies in our power to mitigate it. But we say: If you want to find the greatest degrees and the most desperate forms of suffering, you will find them not in the country parts of this dominion, but in the hearts of our cities. The first proposition is relatively true and nobody on this side of the house attempts to deny that; as a matter of fact, nobody anywhere in the house or of any party attempts to deny it. But is an admission of the present situation, deplorable as it is, tantamount to admitting that the present system is responsible for it? I am prepared to go the length of denying that the admission of the existence of the situation implies any responsibility for it of the present financial or economic system of this country or of our present social system. Its causes are of a nature vastly different. Even were I to go further and admit that our present economic and financial system is incapable of extricating us from the present situation and putting us again upon normal lines, that would not be an admission that it was responsible for the present situation. You are proposing to scrap a system which has been built up through generations and centuries, not from the motive of greed, as suggested by some who are constitutionally misanthropic, or by others who have become misanthropic by reason of the hard conditions through which we are passing, but which has been evolved scientifically with a view to elaborating a system that shall be in the best interests of the world as a whole; which through centuries has built up the civilizations of all civilized countries of the world, and which has drawn together the four corners of the earth by the trade facilities which it has afforded as well as by the facilities for social intercourse which it has made possible. And by reason of the influence which it has had on the development of trade and social intercourse it has bred, perhaps more than any other factor, a sense of the solidarity of
the human race and of the oneness of the human family, which is the greatest asset we possess.
Now it is proposed to scrap all that. Why? Because it has broken down lamentably. Surely it is a pertinent question to ask, why has it broken down? Surely you are not going to scrap it without asking and answering that question to your satisfaction. Has it broken down by reason of inherent defects which render it incapable of functioning under normal conditions and in normal times? Has it proved itself under normal situations unable to fulfil the purpose for which it was designed? Or has it broken down because suddenly it was brought face to face with abnormal conditions, conditions so abnormal that the mind of man never conceived that they could possibly exist? Has it broken down because a strain and burden was imposed on it which no system ever before in the world's history was asked to bear? If that is the explanation, then, Mr. Speaker, we are all astray when we attempt to put upon it the responsibility which hon. members who are behind this resolution seek to place there. It has broken down by reason of an abnormal strain that no system ever devised or that could be devised ever could have stood, the strain which has followed as a result and aftermath of the war. For four years the civilized nations of the world were blasting into nothing gigantic masses of wealth, and not merely destroying that wealth itself, but in its destruction destroying also other forms of wealth; and by the end of the war period there had been heaped up huge, almost inconceivable burdens of international debt on every civilized nation that was imbroiled in that war directly or indirectly. Our financial and economic system had to meet that strain, and in every country in the world it broke down. The great creditor nation to whom was owed a sum which is only a matter of figures on paper, because nobody can conceive of it in his mind, refused to accept anything but gold, and there was not enough gold in all the treasuries of the world to pay that debt. It refused to take goods in payment, and under those circumstances the system broken down. Is it any wonder that it broke down? Is not the marvel rather that it did not break down long before it did, and that the collapse was not more complete and more disastrous than it actually has been?

Therefore I say that both propositions must be proved. Are they true?
In order to ascertain how far these two propositions are true, you will have to look at the causes which created and are continuing the present condition. What are they? They are too many for me to enumerate them all, and they are too intricate and involved.
I shall confine myself to the three major ones.
The first, as I have already mentioned, are the enormous war debts. Nobody denies that, nobody perhaps except a few gentlemen in the southeast corner of the house. The whole
